opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think it really comes down to where we are as a field. Robotics is still very early. We don't yet have the equivalent of a mature foundation model that just works across lots of robots and lots of tasks. The problem is hard enough that no single company, including us, is going to solve it alone by keeping everything behind closed doors.

So when we release model weights, or write up what we've learned in our research, or share hardware designs, the goal is to raise the floor for everyone. If a grad student or a small lab can take a pretrained model, fine-tune it on their own robot with a modest amount of data, and get something working, that's a huge acceleration compared to everyone starting from scratch. And then they discover things, failure modes, new tasks, new tricks for data collection, that feed back into the broader community and ultimately help us too.

There's also a scientific reason. A lot of the questions we care about are open questions: how much data you need, what kinds of data transfer across embodiments, how to get robots to generalize to new environments. You get much better answers when lots of people can test and poke at the same models and compare against shared baselines. Openness makes the science more rigorous.

And honestly, we don't think our advantage comes from hoarding any one artifact. The field is moving fast enough that a model we release today will be superseded in months. What matters more is the team, the pace of iteration, and the infrastructure for collecting data and training at scale. So sharing doesn't cost us much, and it helps the whole ecosystem grow, which is something we need if physical intelligence is going to become real in the world.

r001.rationale: The response says openness helps labs use pretrained models and grow the ecosystem, but does not identify preparing the ecosystem to use future generalist models as a reason.

r002.rationale: It gives no reason involving attracting outstanding researchers or engineers.

r003.rationale: It says no single company will solve robotics alone, but does not state that Finn is more concerned about nobody solving the problem than competitors succeeding.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think there are a few reasons. The first is just that the field of robot learning is still pretty early. If you look at where language models were five or six years ago, there was a lot of open research happening, and that open research is a big part of why things moved as fast as they did. Robotics is at that stage now. We don't think we have all the answers, and we don't think any single company has all the answers. So if we release the weights and the papers and the details, other people can build on it, find the failure modes, and push the whole field forward faster. That ultimately benefits us too.

The second reason is more practical. Robotics has a data problem that's really different from language or vision. There's no internet of robot experience sitting there waiting to be scraped. The data has to be collected physically, on real hardware, and that's expensive and slow. So if we can get more people running models on more robots in more environments, that broadens the base of what the community learns about what works and what doesn't. Releasing open robot designs is part of that. A lot of academic labs can't afford the hardware that an industrial player uses, and if we can lower that barrier, more people can actually participate.

And then honestly, the third reason is about the team and the culture. A lot of us came from academia, and we care about the research being real and reproducible. It's pretty easy in robotics to show a demo video that looks amazing and have no one be able to tell whether it generalizes. When you release the weights, people can just try it. That keeps us honest, and it makes the claims mean something.

I'd add that we don't think the model weights are the moat. The thing that's hard is the combination of data, the infrastructure for collecting it at scale, the iteration loop, and the people who know how to make all of that work together. Those compound over time. So sharing a model checkpoint doesn't give that away. If anything, it attracts the people who want to work on these problems with us.

r001.rationale: The response says openness helps more people run models, participate, and advance robot learning, but does not identify preparing the ecosystem to use future generalist models.

r002.rationale: It says sharing “attracts the people who want to work on these problems with us,” communicating openness as a way to attract talent.

r003.rationale: The response says no single company has all the answers, but does not state that Finn is more concerned nobody will solve generalist robotics than that competitors will succeed.

astra-6.text:
We think there’s a lot of value in making this work something that other people can build on. Robotics is a really broad problem, and any one team can only explore so many tasks, environments, and hardware setups. If people can take a model and adapt it to their own robot or their own application, they can try things that we wouldn’t have thought to try.

And sharing the research and the designs alongside the weights helps make that possible. You want people to be able to understand how the system works, reproduce it, and improve on it. My hope is that this creates a much broader community working on these problems, and that we all make progress faster as a result.

r001.rationale: The response discusses others adapting and building on the work, but does not identify preparing the robotics ecosystem to use future generalist models.

r002.rationale: It mentions creating a broader research community, but does not say openness is intended to attract outstanding researchers or engineers.

r003.rationale: The response expresses a hope for faster collective progress, but does not compare concern about solving generalist robotics with concern about competitors succeeding.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there’s a huge amount of work left to do to make robots useful in the real world, and we’re not going to do all of it ourselves. If people can build on the same models, reproduce the research, and adapt it to their own robots and tasks, we can make progress much faster as a field.

The weights are an important part of that. A paper can describe what worked, but having a model you can actually run and fine-tune makes it much easier to explore a new application. And sharing the robot designs helps people put together the physical system needed to do those experiments. We want to lower that barrier so more people can contribute ideas and discover things we wouldn’t have thought to try.
